utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two brief matters. One, yesterday we made a request regarding a continuance in light of the reaction that I perceived from the Trial Chamber, as I made the request for one month continuance. I went back and I looked at the upcoming witnesses and regrouped my thinking, and I have another proposal, an amended proposal that might be amenable to the Trial Chamber. We could go forward with the witnesses as they are scheduled and perhaps give the Prosecution until, say, as late as June the 13th to get their statements and then after that give us an opportunity, say, at a minimum two weeks break at that point. By that time, we should have the statements, we will have -- hopefully they will be translated and then we can begin to do our work. I think it makes more sense from our standpoint that we go forward and have the time available once we have the transcripts at hand. I don't know if that's feasible on the Prosecution side. They certainly do seem to have quite a few folks working on the case. Plus we're only going half days, and so they can certainly put in -- I understand that the UN Detention Centre is willing to allow them to work on the weekends if need be to use the facilities. The second matter, and I want to apologise to the court yesterday for being less than adequately prepared for my last point that I was raising with respect to Mr. Ruez. I was referring to an exhibit. It was tape number 21, where I was talking about the conversation between General Mladic and Colonel Karremans. I want to make sure that the record is clear that it's tape 21. And then again I wanted to make sure that I was accurate and hadn't misled neither the witness nor the Trial Chamber nor the Prosecution, so I looked at Prosecution Exhibit 21A, and in that exhibit, on pages L0092415 to 6 and L0092422 are references with respect to Mr. Karremans having contacted one, the UN, and secondly, having contacted the BH or BiH government. So I just wanted to make sure that the record is clear and assist you in locating those areas on the transcript. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I know that -- and I thank Mr. Karnavas for his suggestions, but this is the first that we've heard of it. And I believe Mr. Karnavas is concerned more about the statements of Momir Nikolic and Dragan Obrenovic. The Defence for Mr. Jokic is concerned about the fundamental unfairness of proceeding without a final indictment in the case, and so we're opposed to proceeding after this witness, period, until we have all the allegations against our client and can proceed appropriately. So we think that we should go ahead and have a 30-day continuance after this witness so that we can prepare, get the final -- all of the problems. There are several problems hanging around in this case that need to be addressed and maybe within 30 days this will be a trial that is prepared to continue under the Rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe it's a reasonable request. Any response from -- yes. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is an opportunity to say something with regard to what we talked about yesterday, that is, the anticipated announcements and changes of the indictment amendments to be made there with regard to some of the counts. Perhaps, with the Prosecution, we could try to clarify the terminological differences with regard to the indictment. Yesterday when we talked to our client, Dragan Jokic, and I again am making my reservations, in view of the problems with the transcript, that is, the interpretation, we are not quite clear about the difference between seniority command and leadership. According to the military terminology, which both the Prosecution team and we have in front of us, and which has been attached to the report, clearly defines the terms "leadership" and "command." But now we hear a third term, which is priority or authority. Now, does this mean command, commanding authority, in the case of Nikolic, and in Jokic it means something else? We have to clear this up before the deadline for our objections to the amended counts of the indictment. We need to do this with the Prosecution, and with your assistance, Your Honours, but we need to clear this up before the deadline expires. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for letting us know your views on this issue, but this is not a hearing on the amended indictment at this moment. I think the Defence counsel will have plenty of opportunity to make any response to the proposals or applications for the amended indictment at a later stage. Could I hear the initial response from the Prosecution side on all those issues. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, as we stated yesterday, the length of the break we would leave to the court's discretion. However, as Mr. Karnavas indicated yesterday, we would like some time, it would be helpful to the Prosecution to have a break in which we would be able to meet with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic in order to obtain the statements that Mr. Karnavas says that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel slow down, please. MS. DE LA TORRE: -- yesterday that three weeks was not long enough. Sorry. That three weeks was not long enough. He's indicated today that he would be willing to accept two weeks. That's acceptable to the Prosecution. We would simply ask for the two weeks' break that we had previously discussed, and that we had indicated to our witnesses that we would not be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel slow down, please. MS. DE LA TORRE: -- before we resume June 9th. Beyond the two-week break, Your Honour, we would leave that to the court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to be very concise, Mr. Karnavas. We are not going to have a long debate on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Obviously there's a mischaracterisation from the Prosecution. I'm willing to accept the two-week break after I receive -- after I receive, not before, after I receive the transcripts of statements from their witnesses which I'm entitled under the Rules. That's what my position is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, so could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to mention that I apologise to the court. I have not had time to write the request for certification or my written motion to suppress the statements, and if the court will give me a few more days to do that, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. And I think during the procedure of the meeting the evidence you have the full right to orally present your views concerning those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And thank you. I just wanted also the court to be aware that we don't consider going forward with this witness waiving any right that we have to object to proceeding with the trial. We will go forward, but we don't want to waive the right to contest it in writing at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope we can send you home today, but who knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One never knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to bring something to mind today. I noticed yesterday that when you were answering your questions, sometimes you didn't listen to the questions so well and you told your story. I'd like for you to please just listen to my questions today, and if they only need a yes or no answer, would you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will summarise as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel and the witness please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, we will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In my country, when someone says -- you ask a question and they go into a long narrative, we object as non-responsive, but I'm going to assume that you're going to just listen to my questions and answer the question that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. On Wednesday you stated that -- I'm going into your position right now, that you've been on vacation since 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that your new position will be fund-raiser for the Ministry of the Interior of France; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the international cooperation service of Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before that, before you took your vacation and before you came with the OTP, you were an investigator or inspector with the French police department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- the translation is superintendent in the French police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you are superintendent of the French police, that's really an extension of the arm of the Prosecution in France, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Article 1 of our Code of Proceedings is that we act under the control of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you became the investigator for Srebrenica, you were an employee of the OTP at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an employee of the OTP, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as an employee of the OTP, you're just another extension or arm of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also stated that -- well, we don't know -- where did you go to college before you went with the French police department?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the university named Paris 2 in Paris, a law university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did state that you have no expertise in forensics whatsoever; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My expertise is to decide at what moment experts have to be requested to conduct these forensics, but I don't conduct forensics myself, is it correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't have any expertise in it either, only enough to know that you don't know enough to hire someone else?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expertise I have is supposed to be enough to be able to decide at what moment this is needed or not, but I am not an expert, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you came to this courtroom to testify in this case, you didn't provide us with a curriculum vitae, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not requested to do so, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't write a report or a statement for this case, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the only evidence we were given was your prior testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I testified -- this is the fifth time, so I assume you have all the records from -- for these testimonies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's really interesting, because we only have the record from the Krstic case. Can you tell us what other records we were missing?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, you would be missing the testimony I gave for Rule 61 hearing Karadzic, Mladic, June/July '96. In that case you would miss the testimony I gave for the first sentencing of Drazen Erdemovic, end of 1996, and the same thing for the second sentencing of Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we take a break in a moment, may we ask the Prosecution to provide us with that evidence also so that we can review it during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, I've informed by my case manager that they do have copies of all those prior testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Can you provide those documents to the Defence team at this moment. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, they have already been provided. Are you requesting that we give them another copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only one that I was provided, that I'm aware of, might I add, was the testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any records for the furnishment of those documents to the Defence team? MS. DE LA TORRE: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any records for providing those documents to the Defence team? MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour. We have receipts of all of the documentation we provided to the Defence. They have the entire Erdemovic sentencing hearing, as well as the entire transcript from the Rule 61 hearing and the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, my suggestion is that would you please continue your cross-examination, and during the breaks, and you could look into your files to see whether the documents -- and you could revisit it, this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to locate those at the break, but Mr. Stojanovic assures me that we don't have Mladic or Karadzic Rule 61 hearings. So maybe we can try to get a copy of them at our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe during the break you could refurnish those documents to Ms. Sinatra. MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, on the first day you testified at the end of the testimony, of course, we were provided with the script for your testifying here, and the truth is that you're really not an independent witness at all, are you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I leave you the responsibility of what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the whole testimony that you have provided here was a play written by the Prosecution and you're just a mouth piece for them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat the same answer. I leave it to you to think this or say it or claim it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Ms. de la Torre wrote the script and then you acted it out in the courtroom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't act; I testified. I'm not an actor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go to 1995, July 14th. In 1995, there was a serious armed conflict going on between a gigantic Muslim column and the VRS forces at that time, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there was just heavy fighting that it was a concern of the Zvornik Brigade that they would be overrun by this Muslim column; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not exactly the situation. It is the Zvornik Brigade that was worried to be overrun by the Muslim column, not the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought I said the Zvornik Brigade. That's the one I'm really concerned about. The fighting was only like 3 kilometres from the centre of the city in Zvornik, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of the troops, everybody that could hold a gun, was called to defend the city; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there was a public announcement, everybody, no matter what your age, if you can carry a gun, come out and protect our city?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what happened in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that same day, that's the same day that the people from the Bratunac Brigade decided to ship a large group of refugees into the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a decision that was made by Bratunac Brigade. This was a decision made by Drina Corps Main Staff and VRS Main Staff, not Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say "Main Staff," you're talking about the secret service operations that are underneath Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm mainly referring to Mladic himself and his aides from the security branch of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on July 14th, 1995, you know that Dragan Jokic had chosen the black bean and he was the duty officer assigned on that day, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a duty officer -- let me tell you -- well, tell me if I'm right. If the commander or deputy commander or in headquarters the duty officer doesn't do anything, does he?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aside being aware of what is going on around him, indeed, if everyone is present, he has no information to relay, and he is at that moment out of the loop and waiting to enter the loop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the commander or the deputy commander are not present in the brigade is when he has to coordinate communications and send messages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose in your investigation you're familiar with standard or that Zvornik Brigade headquarters there right outside of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not familiar with this building, aside from the outside, since I penetrated that building once, but it was to seize weapons, not to seize documentation, so I only entered the storage room of weapons. I'm not familiar with the brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never went into the different offices within the building?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During that search I was at the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with it through your review of photographs and documents?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know where the duty officer's office was in that building?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no idea. All this part of analysis was conducted by Richard Butler, but I'm not familiar at all with these elements. I know some of important elements that were found at that headquarters, but I didn't participate in the analysis of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the day that they were moving the refugees from the Srebrenica area, Potocari, north toward the Zvornik area, remember we were under -- they were under heavy attack by the Muslim column; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area was under attack of the Zvornik -- sorry -

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I wasn't clear. The Zvornik Brigade was under attack by the Muslim column on July 14th?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade was not really under heavy attack. They were trying to ambush this column, so they were looking for the combat. So they engaged themselves indeed in heavy combat with that column, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the column was coming and the city was here and they went out to protect the city and keep them from overrunning the city; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not exactly the way Colonel Obrenovic explained as the situation during his interview. He explained that there was a main column, the main part of the column was trying to hit Nezuk and they were trying to ambush this column and logically inflict maximum casualties, since it's a military activity, and armed forces going towards them. But that column detached a large group in order to make a fake attack on Zvornik and attract the Zvornik brigade in the defence of Zvornik, so that the rest of the column could make a break through at Nezuk. This is the situation as it was described to us by Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you say that the column made a fake attack on Zvornik, that was to get their forces to come defend the town to enable them to open up the area so they could go through; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So there were -- everybody in Zvornik was concerned that they were going to be attacked by the Muslims; though?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. Everyone said even after that due to the way Zvornik was poorly defended, that column could have taken Zvornik during these days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this operation, which was a legitimate military operation of defending the city -- I'm sorry. Sorry. It was a legitimate military operation at the time. What was coming from the Bratunac area, or from Srebrenica and Potocari, were bus loads of men perceived to be civilians but some were probably in the armed forces at one time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not any longer since long enter the debate about who was a military and who was a civilian since we only, as I already explained, count victims who have gone through a detention process. So whatever happens we are talking about war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about prisoners of war under the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And when you had this bus caravan coming through Zvornik, in the front of the bus you have a white UN APC; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This white APC is spotted both by survivor who was in that column that went to Zvornik and was also spotted by Major Jokic, 14 July, when he saw this large column of buses coming to Zvornik, and the column was headed by an APC, APC indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An APC with United Nations markings on it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A vehicle stolen from the UN battalion in Potocari, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people driving the APC had Blue Helmets on, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know no one who gave that detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even on the buses, didn't you hear from your interviews that there were blue helmets all dispersed through the buses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No Blue Helmets on the buses. The use of the blue helmets was on the stretch of road between Kravica and Nova Kasaba in order to lure the people out of the woods. But once they were prisoners, there was no need any more to make them believe the United Nations was under control, and the descriptions that we got from the men who were guarding the prisoners on board of the buses were either people in camouflage uniforms or some people in camouflage uniforms with white belts that could indicate they were military police people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the white belt indicates MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't indicate MUP. It indicates generally that it's military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain the difference between MUP and military police. Military police are part of the VRS and MUP is not?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP is Ministry of Interior troops, and military police is the police of a military unit, like Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, or also military police attached specially to the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the caravan of buses coming through Zvornik. A caravan of buses carrying prisoners of war, going through Zvornik with a UN APC in the front of it could be perceived as a legitimate military operation, isn't that correct? The question is: Could have been perceived.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the civilians in Zvornik, maybe, yes, but not for the military people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know the military people -- it could have been perceived by the military people, because the caravan didn't stop there, that it was a legitimate military operation, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that all the officers of the Drina Corps at that time were enjoying some victory or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. I think that he's calling for speculation right now. I don't think that he has any facts to base his statement on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, please answer the question put by the Defence counsel directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. de la Torre. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, Defence counsel's question was about what military people could have perceived, which in itself asks him to speculate what the military people might have been thinking or perceiving. As a result, he responded with his own speculation about what he believed that they might have perceived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will be a lot more specific in my question, and I'm sorry if it was unartful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My specific question is: The Zvornik Brigade, on the road going north into Bijeljina, when, if a caravan of buses came by with a UN APC at the lead, anybody in the Zvornik Brigade who just watched this go by could believe that that was a legitimate military operation, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say no. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If you'll just give me a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, there was overcrowding in Potocari, wasn't there, of the places where they were detaining the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the white house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the whole area in Potocari, the DutchBat compound, there was way overcrowding and it was becoming a humanitarian crisis, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but your question was about facilities detaining prisoners of war. Are you talking about the refugees in Potocari, the 25.000?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you just told me that we consider those prisoners of war. Are you considering them civilians, refugees, or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people in Potocari we consider them as refugees. As soon as people had been separated, as soon as people have been arrested or as soon as people have surrendered, they enter a detention process, then we consider these prisoners of war and we do not focus any longer if they were civilians or civilians, potential combatants or combatants in uniform. At that point they are all prisoners versus the people in Potocari, we don't consider them prisoners at that stage. They are refugees waiting, depending who is talking about the situation, waiting for evacuation or for deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a matter of fact, the conditions in Potocari, with, I don't know, 50.000 people, limited into a small area, became a humanitarian crisis, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire operation was to create a humanitarian crisis in this area in order to force the people to go. It's the aim of the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, it was becoming a humanitarian crisis, not enough food, not enough water, not enough medical supplies, not enough space for the people to even lie down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the conditions were there to have these people flee the area as soon as possible, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whenever they were moving these people north, it could have been to relieve the humanitarian crisis, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And bring the prisoners to a better life, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I don't know if you're familiar with earth-moving equipment or military operations during an attack. Are you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never been engaged in combat in the army, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are other reasons for earth-moving equipment to be sent out during combat situation, aren't there? There are reasons such as building latrines if you have a large number of people coming to the area. Wouldn't that be a legitimate reason?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure that would be, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Building trenches to protect the troops; that's another reason, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, they usually have earth-moving equipment poised at the fronts at combat operations for legitimate purposes, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. That's what engineers are for in the army, in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They not only trench; they push up dirt to protect, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One thing they know how to do very well, for example, is to dig a big hole of the size of a tank. That's their specialty. So that only the barrel of the tank points out. And these holes are exactly the size of a secondary mass grave, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is non-responsive. I'm not asking him about the size of secondary mass graves. Can he just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness answered the question. Maybe you don't like the answer yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I think he's editorialising and he's not asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were asking me about what I knew equipment can do, so that's one thing that an engineer unit knows how to do very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the legitimate purposes in a combat zone for earth-moving equipment.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know anything about the chain of command in the VRS at the time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a specialist, but I know a bit about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If there's a commander, the commander has -- is the one who issues orders and controls the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the commander isn't there, it's the deputy commander, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the deputy commander isn't there and we go down to a company, it would be the commander of the company, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the team expert on the regulations of a VRS army. I would prefer having my colleague Richard Butler answer these questions. I'm not a specialist of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a chief of engineering, do you know that that position is merely advisory?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this is a debate we have talked a lot about this issue during the interviews with the suspects. I will not enter this debate in which I am not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll save it for Mr. Butler, then. Let me ask you about this term "terrain restoration." Terrain restoration is a legitimate military term that's used in every military manual around the world, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it doesn't mean just mass burial operations, does it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "mass" would depended on how many bodies have to be taken away from the terrain, so it depends of the battle that occurred before. So yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Terrain restoration is a term used mainly to clean up the battle field after there's been a battle; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's a legitimate military term used throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a legitimate word, yes. It is the technical word used by military people to talk about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that on July 14th there was a plea to the public to provide every bit of earth-moving equipment and equipment that they can to the area of Zvornik? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know that most of the equipment that was used in the Zvornik area was not from the Zvornik Brigade; it was from the other factories and refineries in the area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This I knew, that there was a requisition made by the Zvornik Brigade to civilian companies in order to get earth-digging equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that that requisition was made by the Zvornik Brigade or do you know that it was made by someone from Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good point. That's the one that Mr. Jokic made. He claimed it was done by Main Staff people, indeed. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. No. The requisitions that you're talking about was made by Main Staff. It was not made by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what Major Jokic says. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to talk about another area that we have not talked about in this -- in your interview here. You worked for how many years with Stephanie Frease?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not worked with Stephanie Frease. Stephanie Frease has been attached to -- I mean initially the start of the investigation so during summer 1995, then she came back on the subject around April 1996, and then more or less we never stopped working together until my departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you added it all up, you probably worked with her about six or seven years, would you say?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's good. Now, Stephanie Frease is also an investigator for the OTP, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Her position is research officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a research officer, was she working on one specific area, or conducting the whole investigation with you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: She participated in a lot of aspects, mainly related to the crime base, the witnesses who are crime base. And the main task that she carried on was the analysis of the intercepted communications that we got from BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that Stephanie Frease had no expertise in radio communications or intercepts; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is why we brought in an expert for that topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she was the one doing the investigation, but she had no expertise in that area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't need to be a radio expert to analyse communications and put them in context with the rest of the knowledge that you have of a case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you're dealing with equipment that we're not familiar with, normally ham radio equipment that people brought in of their own and adapted it for these purposes, and you've got three of these listening devices going at one time, and you have somebody trying to transcribe three different conversations going, wouldn't you think you would need some expertise to analyse the communications procedures there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication procedures was one part, to validate the products that we have, transcripts, and the topic of the effort of Stephanie Frease was to analyse these transcripts, whatever piece of equipment took it, that was not her concern. The technical aspect was the concern of a ham radio expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She doesn't have any expertise in ham radio experts, but she does speak B/C/S; is that why she was chosen for this role?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only for that reason. Mainly for the reason that having been on board of this investigation from the beginning, she was very knowledgeable and indeed to understand things sometimes you need knowledge. Most of the time you need knowledge, so she was the perfect person for that part of the activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But she had no expertise in communications procedures?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked earlier, and I believe in one of your interviews about the cooperation of the US State Department by providing those aerial images that you have used over and over again your programme; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me a little bit about the satellite that goes over, and the images that were taken from the satellite? How often does it go by? What kind of satellite is it? Who controls the information?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I have to object. This is a topic that is in the discretion of the United States security and, as I know Mr. Ruez knows, is off limits and is something that is prevented by Rule 70 for us to get into in any great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I think you are asking the witness to speculate. How could he know about those details?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, he used all of those details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: He used. He he's just a user of those products, but I don't think he knows about the details, how those satellites are functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, then perhaps we could go into private session so that I could explore that area a little further, because in our case, there is a possibility that we need more information from this provider also, and I need to know how valuable these were and what other areas of communications they got from the NSA and the US State Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the provider is very clear. You could directly come to the question which is directly related to your client. For instance, you could show a picture saying that, you know, are you sure this is something on the picture? How do you, you know, recognise -- how do you come to the conclusion it's a truck? Or something like this. Rather than asking the sources of those kind of pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I'm interested in the source is not about the pictures. I need to know, and I don't know whether this witness is qualified, but I will probably ask every witness that I think has information about it. I need to know if that satellite or any request has been made for audio intercepts from a satellite or from a military plane that flew over that site on July 14th. The audio intercepts are what we're interested in. It's exculpatory evidence and that's what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you could ask the question like this, but it's very difficult for him to tell you how the function of those satellites, how this picture was taken. Let me turn to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Ms. Sinatra is welcome to take on the United States and try to find this material out. I do not represent the United States. This Tribunal does not represent the United States. And with perhaps a timely motion she can bring the United States into this court and challenge them. We have Rule 70 obligations to the United States and other countries, and this is something that is very important for the -- this Tribunal and that it needs to be done in a way not in a surprise manner, as is being used now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I advise you to skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May I revisit it in written form with the court, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ruez, going back to Ms. Stephanie Frease and tactical radio operators, do you know the difference between a tactical radio operator and a regular communications operator?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't need to do that -- I don't need to know that. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did Ms. Stephanie Frease know that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would bet she does, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I hope that we will have Ms. Frease here to testify for the Prosecution sooner or later. Okay. Let me ask you: On December 14th, 1999, you interviewed and interrogated Mr. Dragan Jokic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Your Honours, just by questioning from this document, I still believe that this document is an illegal document under Rule 95 and we'll continue to contest that. But while we have this witness present, I will take advantage of that. I think I provided copies to the interpretation booths too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, are you familiar with Rule 42, Rule 43, and Rule 63 of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by their numbers, but if you recall me what they are, I might remember, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they have to do with guarantees of rights of suspects during investigation. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And at this point, Your Honour, yesterday I had asked the Prosecution to provide Mr. -- Mr. Ruez testified yesterday that there was a letter from the RS government that complained about the interrogation procedures of the ICTY investigators. I've asked them to provide that to me, and they said that they would. I don't know, before I go into this line of questioning, I should wait and try to get a copy of it from them, if they have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. de la Torre. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, we were faxed a copy of that particular document this morning and it was brought to court shortly prior to beginning. We have it in both B/C/S and English for Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. How many copies do you have? MS. DE LA TORRE: We just have the one, Your Honour. It was brought in shortly before Your Honours arrived. We can make a copy right now or we can simply provide this one to Ms. Sinatra and on a break we can take a copy for ourselves and for Defence -- other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Don't forget us. MS. DE LA TORRE: And Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The usher maybe could help to have this document furnished to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if I might ask the court's indulgence if we could just have our break early and then continue because I promise, I don't think I'm going to go past 1.00 today. We'll have the whole afternoon off if I can just review this document so I can continue questioning Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You are conducting cross-examination. We are in your hands. So we'll resume at 11.20, a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That will be -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra. You got that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Have you received that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did receive it, and I had time to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So you're ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm ready to proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ruez, we were talking about the interview that you did with Mr. Jokic in December of 1999. Do you have a copy of that interview in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May I ask that a copy be provided so that Mr. Ruez can follow along with what I'm talking about. Thank you. I want to offer my apologies to the interpretation department. I was informed that I am speaking way too fast, so I will try to remedy that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know the difference between a witness and a suspect; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A witness will be someone who has information. He could report to the Office of the Prosecutor, in which he is not engaged in criminal activities, versus a suspect would be someone we have reason to believe, because we have information about it, that he might be involved -- having been involved in some crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A witness doesn't require any warnings when you interview him; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean about warnings regarding his rights?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But a suspect does?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, a suspect -- do you know those warnings right off the top of your head?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's try and do it since two years, but so that the person is, first of all, allowed to be -- to have legal representation, that he is allowed to stay silent, that anything he would say would be on the records, that these records would be used in the course of proceedings here in The Hague, that he has also the right to be assisted of an interpreter of his choice. We generally propose one at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's pretty much accurate. When people come in as a witness, many times they leave as a suspect. When do you decide during your interview that you give them the warnings, or do you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might have occurred. I have no precise recollection, yes, but it might have occurred. What happens is that most of the time, we know the position of that person in the chain of command, if it is an officer. We might have no information about the fact that the person committed a crime, but we expect that person to be truthful and explain what he was doing, where he was, who he saw, and things like this. And if after having exhausted a series of questions in order to get an indication of how truthful this witness is or not, if we begin to realise that in fact this person is trying to cover information to protect himself or others, then it begins to become an indication that he might be a suspect, and for the sake of his protection, we would tell him that for the next interview he might be -- his status might change and that if we call him again he might in advance think about consulting and that day come with a proper representative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But most of the time, you're interviewing a witness and you don't give him any rights when he changes and morphs into a suspect until the interview is over and you assess whether he is trying to hide something or not; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not think so. What we would do at one point, it would be to interrupt the interview, inform that person that we are not satisfied with the information we are provided with, that this leaves us unfortunately for him to reconsider his status and that the next time we will summon him it might probably be with the status of a suspect and no longer with the status of a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A lot of times witnesses come in and leave as suspects and suspects come in and leave as accused, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not be able to leave an interview room switching a status from suspect to accused, because the indictment would not be drafted in that time frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the interview of Mr. Jokic on December 14th, 1999. You know that whoever comes to visit you as a suspect has a right to have counsel of their choice; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are aware that on December 14th, 1999, Mr. Jokic came in with an attorney named Krstan Simic; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within a 48-hour period, Mr. Obrenovic came in with Mr. Krstan Simic; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Jevtic came in with Krstan Simic; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also Momir Nikolic came in with Krstan Simic; is that correct? That was 15 December?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right for all of them, but to the best of my recollection, Captain Momir Nikolic arrived alone and waived his rights to Defence counsel, as far as I recall. And I'm not sure at that point, but you have his first interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you're right. I do. They were all interviewed within the 48-hour period. But Jevtic, who was the commander of the Engineering Department, Dragan Obrenovic, who was deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and Dragan Jokic, who was chief of engineering of Zvornik Brigade, were all interviewed within 48 hours, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. That you are sure of your information, I would not say no to that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they all had the same attorney, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were astonished that they would make this choice, but we believed they had good reasons to do so, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that there was VRS meeting of the Zvornik Brigade which recommended that everybody who was a soldier with the Zvornik Brigade be represented by Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been a lawyer of his choice under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these circumstances, these officers do not have to act under orders. They have to take into consideration their own interest, and we make the assumption that when they come with a lawyer, it is indeed the lawyer of their choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I know you make the assumption, and you said you're not familiar with military procedures, so the fact is: If they were recommended to use this one lawyer and they're all in the Zvornik Brigade, that it would not be wise for them not to use the same lawyer, would it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question to be addressed to your client, not to me. I would speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Also the day that you interviewed Mr. Jokic, you had the interpreter Adisa Karamuratovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she is an interpreter hired by the OTP, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Jokic didn't have any other option but to use her, did he?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had an option, as I said, we always offer to either the witness or the suspect to use our interpreter. This is in order to win time, since if the person then would say: I want my own interpreter, we would have to delay the interview, and this is always some problem during missions that have a specific time frame. But he volunteered to have this interview conducted with this interpreter. Had he raised any objection, we would have stopped everything and hired an interpreter of his choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you another question. All these men that you interviewed are citizens of the former Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the legal system in the former Yugoslavia is the continental civil law system; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the continental civil law system, it's my understanding that you have a judge and you have an investigative judge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that during those procedures, that these men were familiar with, they don't have the right to an attorney of their choosing and they don't have a right to an interpreter of their choosing, do they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the former Yugoslav system, but if you say so, I believe you have studied the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me that benefit of the doubt, but in the Yugoslav system, they also -- they don't have the same understanding of the rules of the ICTY, because we have an adversarial system here, basically; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that. Personally, I don't know. I'm not in their position, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and the witness please make breaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the civil law system, the continental law system, all of the evidence is gathered by an investigative judge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to rely on what you say. I believe you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving Mr. Jokic his rights under Rule 42, knowing that he's from a system that's continental law and not familiar with the rules and procedures of the ICTY, you really weren't convinced that he understood those rights, were you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why witness or a suspect is assisted by a lawyer is exactly that, to inform him about all his rights in this new system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's get to Krstan Simic. When you were interviewing Mr. Jokic, isn't it true that Mr. Simic questioned him almost as much as you did?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say so, but the fact is that Mr. Simic interfered several times during the course of the interview, but he did that probably because he thought it was in the interest of his client, I would suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he wasn't just interrupting; he was asking questions of Mr. Jokic too, along with the Prosecutor, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, he was rephrasing questions in order to make sure that Major Jokic understood properly what the meaning of the question was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that Mr. Simic, the next day, was preparing for Mr. Obrenovic's interview, and there is a conflict of interest between those people, wouldn't you say, between those witnesses that you were having?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have an opinion on this. I would leave it to more specialised legal personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people present at this interview were Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Harmon, Mark Harmon and Stephanie Frease and you, is that correct, plus the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it common for you to go out and interview these witnesses in the many years that you've been there and have them all be represented by the same counsel?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they believe this is the best way to serve their interest, there is nothing we could do at that stage to oppose it, as far as I know. For us, it was an obvious way for them to make sure that no one would go off line, and this is the reason why we believed they had made the choice to have the same lawyer, in order to harmonise their versions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in order to harmonise their versions, which means that if a conflict of interest was between the two of them, then one person might be harmed at the other one's expense; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the choice they make. Then they have to suffer the consequences of it if it is a wrong choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you see a red flag come up when they were all represented by the same lawyer? You didn't recognise a potential conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the mentality that one can imagine which merged these people together, I think we have hard time to transpose our standards in their way of doing. So we were more seeing this as a kind of a melting of interests than a conflict of interests, as far as I recall this, and as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you have a hard time putting yourself in their position, just think of what a hard time they had putting themselves in your position as an investigator for the OTP when they didn't know the legal parameters.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal representative was there to explain to them all these legal parameters. This is why he was supposed to be there also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I just mention the part about Mr. Simic interrogating Mr. Jokic, and would you look at page 25 of the interview. KS, KS, KS is Simic; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. McCloskey says: "I think it's not working. We need to get the rules down, who is asking the questions and who is answering." Doesn't he say that, line 27?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to Mr. Nikolic's interview: Are you sure you gave him his warnings and he waived his right to an attorney?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by reviewing the document would I be able to give you an answer. I don't remember specifically. My instinct answer indeed would be yes, but if you ask, maybe probably something was wrongly done there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll check that in a minute. As a police officer in France, did you attend any special training programmes that taught you the language of interrogation and how to get the answers that you wanted out of the people you were interviewing?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such a course does not exist, as far as I know, in France.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through your interrogation through the years, haven't you learned how to manipulate the witnesses to have them say what you want them to say?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not at the extent of an American defence attorney. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Oh, I think he's criticising counsel, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not criticising. I'm making compliments. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just one moment. Also in this interview, if you'll look on page 53 and page 55 and page 58. 53, line 10, Dragan Jokic: "But Judge, can I tell you about something that I haven't seen?" And then 55, again Dragan Jokic refers to Mr. Harmon or Mr. McCloskey as judge, doesn't he, on line 21: "I don't know, Judge. I want to tell you what I heard exactly." And then on page 58, finally, Mark Harmon says: "All right. Take the roadblocks out." Line 24 -- "Were you Pete." And then Peter McCloskey says: "Before I start too much, I just want to clear one --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sorry

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "You refer to Mr. Harmon and I, I think several -- three times as Judge or Mr. Judge." And this was through page 58 of the interview, that the legal representatives for the OTP and the investigators allowed Mr. Jokic to think that they were the investigative judge, like in a continental law system, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first point that it's indeed ICTY Prosecutors who pinpointed that vocabulary mistake made by Major Jokic, and that indeed it took three times to hear this word before that there was a reaction, because initially, as far as I recall this, we were considering that it was just a kind of mistake on the word, not a misunderstanding about who was who. But on the other hand, but then I would have to speculate on the psychology of Mr. Jokic, I don't think that for him it made a big difference being in front of a judge or a prosecutor from the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't think there's a big difference between the investigative system and the continental system and being in front of an adversarial prosecutor who is going to take everything you say, put it on record, and use it against you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't think that that had any influence on the declarations that Major Jokic was making that day. He had, I think, much other concerns that day than getting a legal course on the difference between American and Yugoslav -- I mean, sorry, civil law and common law aspects. And anyhow, we had to expect that his Defence counsel would be the one teaching him all these differences prior entering the interview room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true that you knew that Mr. Simic didn't ever meet with Mr. Jokic? Is that true? He never prepared him for this interview?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no insight on what was happening at the moment we were sending the summons. We had no insight at all about what was happening behind the scene before these people were making contact directly with us in Banja Luka, at the place we had the appointment with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know that it was a Main Staff VRS meeting where they were told to have Mr. Simic represent them before the ICTY in Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm we had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when somebody is ready to end an interview and they say: I'm really tired. I want to end the interview. Do you normally end the interview when they ask you to?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would, except if there is something important that would need to be finalised, we would just make sure we do it quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is no, you don't necessarily end it when he says to end it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I balance the end sight. It's not a no answer. I mean, I don't have a precise recollection that this happened, but it certainly might have happened and could very well be depending on the circumstances that either we would say "No problem. We stop everything and we make a contact tomorrow," for example, or because of time constraints in the mission, would say to the person, "Listen, we still have ten minutes to go through one or two questions. We'll make short and you'll be free in ten minutes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a second interview with Mr. Jokic on April 1st, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. McCloskey was present, and someone named Ms. Jan Kruszweski?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jan Kruszweski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigator from the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mark Harmon was not present at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you turn to page 69 of the second interview.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On line 9. Mr. Jokic: "In order not to bring myself into trouble in the confusing situation, I am overtired. May I not answer to this question? I am sure that Colonel Obrenovic will answer it tomorrow." And then you keep asking -- you keep asking questions, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said page 69, line --?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Line 9.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the proper page, I think. I have transcript 903, at the end, at the number of the page, on top right. I have another text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There must be a mix-up here.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But never mind. I don't need to have the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, does that sound about like what happened? And then you asked: "I agree totally with that. Sure. Your choice." And then Mr. Jokic says: "If you believe me, I am overtired being questioned. In that sense, I would rather not answer." And you continue the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to be fair to this witness, could Madam Registrar furnish that document to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is P26/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. What is your point here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's start back on page --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I say to him: "Okay. In that sense, since you're overtired, we are going to terminate this interview. I will show you two photographs in this interview."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you keep going, don't you? In fact, you go on to --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Indeed you are right. We continue, indeed, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until finally his counsel says, on page 71: "We are not going to consult. We are tired," line 9. Then you continue for several more pages.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Be aware that one page like this is what, is one to two minutes of talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One to two minutes of talking. Should we time ourselves and see how much information we can get into one to two minutes of talking, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe we should make this test if it is useful for the course of the truth in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, I believe that you went on for about ten more pages even after Mr. Jokic said he was tired, Mr. Jokic said he was tired, and his lawyer said they were tired and wouldn't answer any more questions. Okay. I want to go to one incident that happened - and I just want to refresh your memory about it. On the first interview with Mr. Jokic, on page 77, JR, I suppose that's --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Line 12. "It's five hours and 30 minutes. We'll make a break." Now, do you remember during this break that an IPTF officer with a machine-gun came into the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, I don't know; two, this is not possible. IPTF officers never carry machine-guns. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was SFOR, excuse me, an SFOR officer with a machine-gun, came into the interview room.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- where was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey must have been present then too.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of any SFOR officer or SFOR personnel inside the building where we were. We had some security in the vicinity, but no one close to the building where we were in Banja Luka. So I'm really wondering about this. I have no recollection of it and I don't see what an SFOR person would do in that place that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember Mr. Jokic going outside of the interview room with your interpreter at that moment?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't specifically recall him -- you mean outside of the room or outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside of the room, standing outside in the hall. And you don't remember Mr. Krstic telling Mr. Jokic that he was going to be taken away to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, sorry, but for me this sounds absolutely ridiculous. When we were doing these breaks, generally Mr. Jokic had a separate talk with Mr. Simic. We were going at a distance of them and not to be heard by them regarding whatever comments we wanted to make among ourselves about what already happened, what we would wish to see happening, and things like this. But we were probably not even at site contact. We would go to the bar area, for example, and they would stay at some part of the corridor or the reverse; they would go to a place where they can talk quietly and we would be elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
