utterances.text: So during this break, which only lasted, I assume, a few minutes, it doesn't say. Nine minutes was the break; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that nine minutes, Mr. Jokic was standing outside with the interpreter. You wouldn't have heard her say to Mr. Jokic: "Poor you. Do you have someone to take care of your son?"

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you saying that I first understood that Mr. Simic was making this comment to Mr. Jokic, and now you are telling me that who said that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic first said: "Mr. Jokic, you're going to be taken to The Hague." And then the interpreter said: "Poor you. Do you have someone to take care of your son?"

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter never stayed in the vicinity of both the defendant -- I mean, the suspect and his client during these breaks. The interpreter is an ICTY personnel, would never stay next to the suspect and his lawyer. I can state that this is a bold lie. This interpreter never would have acted like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then we'll see if we can get Mr. Simic to come in and testify about the events. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be glad to see him talk about this, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there weren't 20 to 25 SFOR officers or soldiers waiting out in that common area that you referred to as the bar?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. That day, I had requested the British base nearby to have some forces in the vicinity of the building, but out of sight of the building. We wanted area security around that building, specifically that day, and specifically because of the fact that Mr. Jokic that day was the witness. I wanted to take some security measures in case indeed something significant would happen during this interview and that we would have to take security measures, not only for us, but also for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you just said that you didn't have any armed soldiers in the vicinity at the time I'm talking about, 5.00 and 29 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mixing two things. Let's reboot everything. That day, for the sake of this interview, I did request that the British base nearby to provide us area security, that means armed people in the vicinity ready to intervene if something happens, but out of sight, not visible. Inside this building was no SFOR personnel requested by us. I would not say that -- it's not a prohibited area for SFOR. It's a UN headquarters in Banja Luka. But there was no one inside the building aside our own UN security officers to deal with our subject. So if ever there was some SFOR soldier there might be for any kind of meeting with some IPTF or whatever UN person, but it was disconnected from our interview process.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment, I don't know if Mr. Ruez has had an opportunity to review the letter that he referred to in his testimony yesterday. It's a letter from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence, dated 26th June, 2000. I believe we have it marked as Defence 3 Exhibit something or other.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. This letter is marked D2/3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you've had an opportunity to look at this letter, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. What I remembered of it was by heart when I talked about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you like to take a moment to review it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I still recall roughly the content of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you'll notice the date of the letter, 26/6/2000. That is just two months after Mr. Jokic's last interview, isn't it, since he was interviewed in April?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disconnect this letter from the interview of Mr. Jokic. This letter is covering our entire process, so already six months of interviews conducted in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, could he just answer the question. I asked him whether this was after the date of the last interview with Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, this question could be answered by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is referring to the series of interviews by the ICTY since, I think, December of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the second page of this letter -- by the way, the letter is signed by Manjolo Milovanovic; is that right, and is he the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It's a letter that was addressed from Ministry of Defence to Ministry of Justice, in order to request Ministry of Justice to complain to the ICTY Prosecutor about our behaviours, and in fact force us into behaviour. The letter was never sent. It was leaked in between these two ministries and to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, non-responsive. I didn't ask him anything else about the letter. I'm doing the questioning at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Would you direct the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, try to keep your answer as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, on the second page, Mr. Ruez, and I'm going to go through this in detail, "According to their allegations, during interviews, human dignity and spiritual integrity are being insulted." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recognise the propaganda phrasing of these officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked him if that's what it said. Would you instruct him not to respond unless I ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Interviews are exhausting, up to 12 hours' duration. Threats of arrest are incessantly resorted to. It is impossible to consume food and in general there is a humiliating treatment on the part of the investigators." Is that what it says, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. "And further, in regard to this, and in accordance with Articles 12, 13, and 14 of the RS constitution, Articles 5, 6, and 10 of general declarations on human rights, as well as with the resolution 217(A)(3) of the General Assembly dated 1/12/1948, we demand that you inform the prosecutor's office of The Hague Tribunal about this so that a fair and correct treatment during interviews would be provided." Was that their demand?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the content of the letter, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next paragraph: "We also deem it necessary that the interviewed persons should be able to read and sign the minutes of the interviews or be provided with phono-taped records of interviews," and the next paragraph just asks that you pay the expenses of the witnesses that you call to come interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right. I read the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to something else now, Your Honour. If you'll just give me a second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to the seizing of documents. Were you involved in the search and seizure of the Zvornik Brigade, of the documents in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of the Zvornik Brigade. We conducted simultaneously two searches, one at the Zvornik Brigade. That search was headed by John Ralston, chief of investigations, and I was in charge of Bratunac Brigade. So that day I was at the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they were done simultaneously, you mean they were both executed on December 14th, 1999, while Dragan Jokic was being interviewed; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not possible, because, as you said, I was present at the interview of Dragan Jokic. I could not be the same day doing a search of the Bratunac Brigade. I don't remember the date of the search of the Bratunac Brigade, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the Zvornik Brigade that was searched on December 14th, 1999, while Mr. Jokic, Mr. Obrenovic, and Mr. Jevtic were in Banja Luka at your summon.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a memory in my souvenir, we were conducting these searches simultaneously, the same day. One team was doing the Zvornik Brigade and we were doing Bratunac Brigade. I couldn't be -- I mean, I don't -- I don't see how it is possible, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it sometime in late 1999, though, that the documents were seized?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The searches were conducted in 1998. Wait a minute. Yes, 1998, yes, sure, the searches of the two brigades were conducted in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of Standard headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the occurrences of the indictment occurred in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What indictment are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The indictment alleging all the crimes that occurred at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995, November 1995, is the date of the indictment of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's July 1995, but ...

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. No. The indictment for Srebrenica is September 1995, for General Mladic and President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have two indictments in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have from 1995 to 1998, before you seized any of the documentation of the Zvornik Brigade, isn't there room for people to plant their own documents during that time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All speculations are possible in such a time frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the SFOR representatives you sent a request to the Minister of Defence and then it's three days before you actually search those premises, but they have three days' warning that you're coming?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If indeed such a thing happened, it was without our knowledge, because our way to deal with such operations together with SFOR is to give the warning at the moment, more or less at the moment we penetrate the brigade, and this is what was supposed to happen that day. We were in position to start the search, then we were receiving the information that all the demands had been passed through the relevant ministries, and timing the moment when the brigade commander or the duty officer receives the instruction from its ministry to let the search happen, we try to minimise that delay at about half an hour, and then we come in and start the search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it sounds like you're dealing with a giant bureaucracy there. There is advance warning to the people in the brigade before you're able to go in there and seize the documents; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, no. But this question should be asked, in that case, to those who planned the operations together with us at SFOR. But we don't -- we try to minimise these delays, for reasons that are obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, we were provided with an interview that you gave to the French Legislative Commission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you given other interviews before or after that time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to commissions or to other organs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the press.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since 1995 -- 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what articles you've had -- interviews you've had published since then?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long evolution, but in 1995 it was mainly press coverage of missions we were conducting in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name the newspapers or the source?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many news agencies were following our missions in 1995 and 1996 -- I mean 1996, because 1995 we were not in RS, CNN, Reuters, others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we weren't provided with any of those interviews either.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not interviews. These were images.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did you personally give any interviews to the press from 1995 until today?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those press services?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one you are referring to is the one that I gave -- I don't remember exactly the date. You will remember -- to Belgrade newspaper, named The Interview, a weekly magazine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not familiar with that and have not received a copy of it. At the next break, would it be possible for the Prosecutor to provide us with a copy of that interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we have to know how important those interviews are. Secondly, if you ask some questions, only under context of how those interviews are conducted, I don't think it's necessary for you to have those interviews. But if you're going to the contents of these interviews, I believe it will be fair to furnish the witness with that copy of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I don't know whether I would want to go into the content of the interview until I see it, because I haven't been provided the interview by the Prosecution. And we were -- we are supposed to be provided with all statements, interviews, information, c.v.s, reports, anything that is a product of this witness in relationship to Srebrenica and 1995, and I have not had an opportunity to look at that. And maybe I wouldn't want to question from it, but before we let this witness go, I would like to have the opportunity to look at it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear from the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. de la Torre. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, the Prosecution has an obligation to provide the Defence with any prior statements of the witness which are in its possession, which we have done. This is considered open-source material, to which Ms. Sinatra and the Defence has as much access to as the Prosecution in this particular case. If we had a copy of that interview, we would have provided it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have it now, at this moment? MS. DE LA TORRE: No, Your Honour. I'm not aware of any such interview, and we certainly don't have a copy in our possession or we would have previously provided it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, Ms. Sinatra, in this situation, it seems to us that we won't get those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'll be going through one more break. If I do, then I will try to find it on the Internet myself and review it, now that I know it exists. I didn't know it exists until my questions. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could, but, you know, we have to make a break at 1.00. We only have 45 minutes left. So are you suggesting that we'll start in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to wrap it up before 1.00. I would like to have an opportunity to review that. Maybe I could let my interpreter go look for it while I'm finishing my questioning, if that would be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'll excuse him from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean you'll go --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No. Mr. Djukic will go look for it, if he'll be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you gave an interview with the French parliamentary commission on February 22nd, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were already retired from the ICTY at that time or were you still the chief investigator for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never retired, but I was still at the Office of the Prosecutor at that time, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it allowed for you to give interviews like that while you're still employed by the ICTY as chief investigator?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll wait for the translation. I was cleared to do so by the deputy Prosecutor of the OTP, Graham Blewitt. And it is not really an interview. I mean, it's a parliamentary commission. It's not a press organ or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you come to certain conclusions and opinions in this interview that are outside the scope of your investigation with the ICTY, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a courtroom either. It's a parliamentary commission. So in these circumstances, you can express opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the interview in front of you, or have you seen it, reviewed it recently?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received a copy of it, and to be honest, I didn't read it back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say that you talk about evidence that has not been submitted to the ICTY because it can't be relied upon fully?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of it was is that I gave what I call the standard briefing, which is in fact what I gave here, as a summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Non-responsive. I asked him if he stated that he was putting evidence before this commission that was not considered reliable before the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to re-enter the details of what I said. It could be that I said things that were not still -- possible. I emphasise possible. I cannot say yes or no, but I say possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your interview, did you also insinuate to the French parliamentary commission that some of these deaths and murders in Srebrenica could have been prevented if the SFOR and American forces would have supported the Dutch troops?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also state that the request for the air raids and other raids are not being investigated by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that the investigation, the criminal investigation I was in charge of starts 11 of July, after the airstrikes. I say that since my first testimony in this Tribunal in June 1995. That was meaning for those who were listening attentively, that the goal of this investigation was, it is an investigation on the crimes committed after the fall of Srebrenica. It is not an investigation on why and how this UN enclave fell. This is why I always insist on the fact that this investigation starts 11 of July, after the airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might ask for an instruction here. He is testifying -- he is -- I have his testimony in front of. Maybe it's not the purpose of the ICTY investigation to determine only the crime that was committed at Srebrenica, but he's not talking to the ICTY now. He's giving an interview in front of the French parliamentary commission, and he did state that requests for air raids and other raids are not being investigated by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say that or not?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to take exactly the statement and check the translation from French into English, but what I always used to say in such circumstances is exactly what I just said before. The investigation I was in charge of, for me, in fact yes, I put my own limit on this, is we start 11 July, after the airstrikes. And this is probably what I repeated again here. Here also I have to add that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might interrupt right here. I didn't ask him to add anything. I think he's editorialising. If he would like a copy of this to have in front of him, I would be happy, and this is my only copy that I have in the courtroom at the moment, but I'd like to introduce this into evidence to describe Mr. Ruez's credibility, and I'd like for the court to see it eventually. But I don't have another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I believe that answer of this witness is responsible. We get what he said in his testimony. And as I said to Mr. Karnavas, that if there's any documents you are going to use which is not on the list of the documents provided by the Prosecutor, you had better furnish us with that document before you conduct your cross-examination, so that the Trial Chamber, the witness could know exactly what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do remember you saying that, and I humbly apologise to the court. I didn't expect Mr. Ruez not to remember what he said in his interview. But I will most certainly file a copy with the Registrar and provide copies for the court, unless you would like to take a break and let me make copies now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: To make copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make a break for ten minutes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra. Have you got copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. I apologise. The only copy I had to make from has some personal pen scratching, but nobody can read my handwriting anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It's true. Okay. If I may continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, now that you have a copy, do you see down one, two, three, four, five, six, you said that there were requests for air raids and other raids that were not being investigated?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that the airstrikes are not part of the investigation I'm in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And on page 2, you do confirm that the NATO equipment was used by the Main Staff operation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The equipment was stolen from the Blue Helmets and was used.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I orient you on something that you asked me previously and you are not asking me now, regarding information that was not submitted to the ICTY? And I'm talking about page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can re-ask the question. I prefer to leave it in question and answer form, if you don't mind. I know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From page 1, I believe you said you were talking today but you are talking about part of the investigation that has not been submitted to the ICTY and cannot be fully relied upon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is written, paragraph 3, but I need to give some explanation about it, because this relates to only paragraph 4 and paragraph 5. As soon as I start paragraph 6 I am in information that had been provided to the ICTY. This is why I say that now I can talk about it more openly, because we did disclose I say 80 per cent - it's an estimate - of the information in our possession to the public. So when I say I'm going to talk about information that cannot be relied upon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please he slow down?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- summary of the ethnic cleansing part of the events in that area, starting in 1992. And this was not part of the investigation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters have difficulties to follow you. If you read something, please slow down and make a pause after each sentence.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I'm cautioning the people who are listening on the fact when I talk about 1992 to 1995, I'm talking -- let me pardon the expression as a tourist, not about something I have investigated but something that is supposed to be more or less, let's say, common knowledge. And there is a mistake, paragraph 5, the Vuk Karadzic massacre --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to object. This is not question and answer. I didn't ask him to correct the whole interview all I asked him to do was to comment on the part that there was information that was not relied upon by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, if you think you have answered the question to you by Defence counsel, you could stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 6, last paragraph, when you say, "As you said, Minister, nothing is written about the orders," you're referring to the fact that the whole operation in Srebrenica was a Main Staff secret operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you say, "Nothing is written about the orders given." The orders were certainly oral. Is that what you meant in the Srebrenica operation, the murder operation is what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't state it was secret. I just said it was oral instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to page 8, and on page 8 you talk about that there was an oral requisition for all private vehicles to be gathered by means of a public appeal on the radio. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that most of the transport companies were the Drinatrans and Centrotrans which are private companies, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And mostly private vehicles provided for this, not military equipment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And look on page -- the top of page 9, if you would. I know that you're referring to the secondary mass graves, but it's clear that here, although you deny saying "secret," secret is the same as confidential operation carried out by Main Staff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make a difference between the two words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree that it was a confidential operation that was not publicly known at the time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be one, but it didn't work exactly like that for the first phase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go down to the last paragraph on page 9. It's true, and you admit, that there was no evidence of any prior planning for the murder operation; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the state of our knowledge when I made that declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it true that all of this was done on the spur of the moment?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you did say that there was no evidence of any prior planning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't translate in the way you put it, spur of the moment. No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. No prior planning. I'll accept that. That's correct. Thank you. Now, in this article, you talk about the air defence component being very significant and that you know that one of your missions will be to look into that. That's at the top of page 10. But we're not investigating any of the airstrike defence mechanism of SFOR or NATO, are we?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but this is related to a completely different context. So if I answer only by yes and no, I will never be able to provide you an explanation on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this document is going to be provided to the Trial Chamber, and they can come to their own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And of course, Your Honours, I can't go into any questioning on the American State Department or NSA photographing or possibility of other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends, you know. If the witness mentions in this interviews, you could ask questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you do say that you asked the American State Department for the access to aerial imaging and that they gave you the aerial imaging from their satellites, photography, which enabled you to find these disturbed -- areas in the ground; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said everything what you are saying with the exception of satellite. This is a word I would never use. Our Rule 70 obligation is to refer to any aerial imagery with the word "aerial imagery."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I refer you to page 10, paragraph 4, last sentence: "I suppose that you used satellite photography." So that was a word that was mentioned by Francois Lamy. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was not your term, you're right. But do you have any information, personal information from your experience and your investigations dealing with the satellite imagery, I mean the aerial imagery, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand properly your question about personal information about this imagery. I don't see the point. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you review the information that was given to you by the United States intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your review of that information, were you told how that information was gathered?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not need to know how the things are gathered. We just need to have elements that assist us. Going on the ground in the most safe possible way in order to reach the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't ask whether he needed to know. I asked whether he knew, whether he discovered during his investigation how the information was gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I think when the witness answers a question, he's entitled to give some short, concise explanation of that answer. We are satisfied with his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11, you talk about the platforms that took those aerial images not flying every day. Was that referring to satellite or aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it's clear that if I say "platforms" that we are not flying; we are talking about aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. That's why I was asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Platforms that don't fly every day can only be aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there are satellites that only rotate once every two days too, so it could be either one. On page 12 -- I'm sorry. On page 12, on the second paragraph, you agree that the executions were carried out very quickly after there was a feeling of panic within the Main Staff of the VRS; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that there was at that point a lack of volunteers to conduct the killing operation, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about volunteers. I was asking you about -- you describe a feeling of panic. Are you talking about there was a feeling of panic and decisions had to be made very quickly? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring about the stress experienced by Colonel Beara during these days, since his task was to find people to kill all the prisoners and he had difficulties finding those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also, on page 13, you go into a semi-conspiracy that you're insinuating that maybe the casualties at Srebrenica would not have been so high if the BiH government hadn't withdrawn Naser Oric on the relevant days of this indictment. Is that what you're insinuating?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was here reacting to a widespread conspiracy theory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the widespread conspiracy theory doesn't have to do with Naser Oric being withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is related to that, but I just referred to this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That that was --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rumour of conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you don't say rumour here. You say: "They did not need to bother doing this, since it was actually the Bosnian government which withdrew Naser Oric, their best officer from the enclave." Isn't that what you say? That's not a rumour that you're stating here before the French parliamentary commission, is it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read back this, please. No. I just mentioned the fact that despite of -- I mean, I'm referring to attempts made by the Serb side to eliminate Naser Oric from the enclave, and I just add here that though they did not succeed, they reached indirectly their result, since Naser Oric was withdrawn with his best officers from the enclave. That's the only thing I'm saying here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An especially strange measure to the extent that without this person and his assistants, it was clear that the wish to defend the enclave was severely limited; isn't that what you say?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I express my opinion on this issue here, yes. But it's my opinion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You even go into conspiracy theory in the next paragraph, don't you? In fact, you state that: "It's possible to say today that the Bosnian authorities indirectly took part in the legal security of a large number of the perpetrators of the crime by not presenting evidence that they had in the clearest and most honest form possible." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's unfortunately true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph on page 13, you agree that the operation itself was a creation of General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that it was essentially an intelligence and security procedure; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I give my opinion on this topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I have no more questions from this document, Your Honours. And I'll try to wrap it up real quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, have you ever heard of a psychological term called conspiracy of silence?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is conspiracy of silence something that they came up with after World War II, when the Germans, although the local people may have suspected that something was going on, everybody was too afraid and too helpless feeling to do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure that there was conspiracy of silence in Germany after World War II. I think it was exactly the opposite; everything was coming on the table, the opposite of the situation we are experiencing here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me say: While the crimes were unfolding during World War II, this term, psychological term, conspiracy of silence, was what they used during the unfolding of the crimes in World War II; is that correct? If you know. If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not busy with World War II here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Mr. Ruez, have you sought any -- since you retired in 2001, have you been under any psychological care yourself?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not retired since 2001. I'm on a leave of absence of my administration. And I've not been under psychological care until now in any circumstance yet, yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well, yesterday you said that you were so wrapped up in the case and so obsessed that you really couldn't view the questioning objectively. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that on the questioning by Mr. Karnavas, you said you couldn't answer that question objectively. And I can't remember the exact question.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to recall me that point. It might be on one detail, it could be, but I would not expand the conclusion like you do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back and just clean up some various questions I have left. Are you familiar with the requisition procedure that is used in the military to get authority to use equipment or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic educated us on this aspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not familiar in general in the military; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these written mission plans, I know that Mr. Karnavas has asked for them, but I believe they're most important for the days of July 14th, 15th, and 16th, or shortly thereafter, for the seizure and search of the Zvornik Brigade. We would like to request that you provide us with those written mission plans for the search and seizure of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't request me. Request the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay. I'll request through you to the Prosecutor, because you're the one who wrote the mission plan, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will fulfil the instructions of the Chamber and of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may -- would you please -- I'm asking that we be provided with those written mission plans for the search and seizure of the documents relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we have already discussed this issue yesterday, and the Trial Chamber will make a decision after cross-examination, after we finish the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that I have honoured my obligations to the Trial Chamber. It's a few minutes until 1.00. I want to thank Mr. Ruez for being here and answering our questions, and I'd also like to re-urge our request that after final indictment in this case and our new investigations, if further developments occur, that we may need to recall Mr. Ruez, depending on the changes that come up in our final indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. We'll take your remarks into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have five minutes left, so our suggestion is that we break now and resume at 2.30. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the interview of the witness with the French legislative commission is marked D3/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume at 2.30 in the same courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any re-examination? Ms. De la Torre. MS. DE LA TORRE: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution does not have any re-direct questions for Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MS. DE LA TORRE: We were advised, Your Honour, that you would prefer -- the court would prefer that we offer our exhibits at the end of re-direct. We can either do that now or after the Judges' questions, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we should give some time for the Judges to ask questions, which might trigger off some other questions. MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, can you tell us: What was your mandate? What was the sphere of your responsibility when you have been performing your function of investigator in the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mandate initially was to go to the Tuzla area and assess the rumours that were reaching the Office of the Prosecutor in the days that followed the fall of the enclave, the 11th of July, so it was a kind of preliminary mission. The fact is that a bit later on there was no real mandate. It was an assessment mission that turned into an investigative mission. But to be honest, without any clear mandate. I invented a bit the mandate. This is why I said previously that it was a self-limitation when I said that the investigation started 11 of July, after the airstrikes. But to be more precise on the answer: Sometime later, when the structure was created to deal with this topic, the mandate was very clear and large, that is, to continue with investigation as far as we could go on with it, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And later on, you were acting on the basis of your free will, as freelance, or you had a mandate?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the frame of that mandate, that is, to follow up with the investigation, I was not freelance. I was putting on paper all our proposals for missions on the ground in Republika Srpska or in Bosnia, if it was interview missions. These mission requests were assessed by the hierarchy and cleared to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But what do you mean, to clear up what happened?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say cleared to happen, I mean that I was getting authorisation from the Office of the Prosecutor to fulfil this mission plan. So deal with the administrative aspects, travel, plus all what was linked with the mission request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the mission request? What was the aim of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the time of the investigation, it was initially mainly missions aimed to interview victims; then it turned into continuity of interviews, until, let's say, the reservoir of witnesses, of key witnesses, was emptied. I'm talking here about mainly the survivors, because for the rest of them, we could continue doing interviews during years, because of the amount of people we are talking about. And then missions in order to go on the ground, identify places, and all the aspects dealing with admin., security, and everything. I mean I could give you the layers of what happened in this investigation during years, because there are clear levels that can be identified, but I don't know if this would satisfy your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. And so one of your tasks were to -- was to identify the potential witnesses; yes?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primary task indeed was to identify key witnesses. Then as soon as we could access the area where these crimes occurred, so not earlier than January 1996, then the main goal was to try to identify the places where the events described by the witnesses occurred, and begin to find out during these missions what could confirm their declarations, and also looking into what would make it impossible for them being witnesses of such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you manage to identify the survivors of the Srebrenica massacre?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. The persons within the team we call survivors are only those who survived mass executions. I mention that because in the press in 1995, and also in 1996, people were presented as being survivors, though they were not direct victims of executions. As far as we are concerned, we consider that approximately 10, if I am -- maybe it's 9 or 11, but I think it's 10, 10 people we consider having survived the mass executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How many mass graves, in total, were discovered by your team?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question in reality, because when we are talking about primary crime scenes and primary mass graves, we in reality talk sometimes about only one mass grave, if it is a very large one, but sometimes we are talking about multiple mass graves. An example, Branjevo Farm mass grave, primary mass grave is one huge mass grave, but Glogova is two sites, and each site includes approximately five to six graves, mass graves. So we have as many mass graves as execution sites, since the large execution sites were all associated with burial process in the immediate vicinity of the execution site. And when we are talking about the re-burial process, so the spreading of all the bodies robbed from the primary mass graves to be then relocated in secondary mass graves, I don't think I'm wrong when I state that we have identified 30 secondary mass graves in the course of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And how many remains of the dead bodies and their parts were discovered in these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer to leave that answer to investigator Dean Manning, who compiled all the information in connection with the findings in the graves, but at this point I could only give a figure in connection with the figure that was given after and during the proceedings of the trial of General Krstic, and that was at that time just about 2.000 bodies, minimum number of individuals who were exhumed, and the assessment of Professor Wright, who exhumed some of secondary mass graves was that that number would finally be above 5.000, the day they would have finalised the entire exhumation process. Unfortunately, that process is still not over today, in 2003, and I'm sorry to expand on your question, my honour, but it's a bit the same situation as when we are discussing with Lawyer Karnavas the possibility to access these brigades. Yes, we had some indications that we should do this in 1995, but we could only do this in 1998. But if you look at the exhumation aspect of this case, we started in 1996. We are now in 2003. Eight years after the events, we have located probably 95 per cent of all these graves. There are still a number of them that have to be exhumed yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: Did your team ever find the identical shell casings at different execution sites?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the sake to be precise, I will have to relay that question to Dean Manning, who has compiled all the data. All the material that was found around the execution sites, inside the primary mass graves, and also inside secondary mass graves, I'm talking mainly about shell casings, cloth, and ligatures, plus additional elements, depending on specific locations, all this material has been forwarded to scientific labs and the results of their findings have been filed -- their reports have been filed during the trial of General Krstic. And yes, indeed, a lot of connections were made linking primary execution sites with primary mass graves, and later on, primary mass graves with the secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ruez. I only have one question, and for the parties to follow, this is page 489 in the transcript from Monday, the 19th. And it's a question put to you by Ms. de la Torre, at line 22. And you answered something that I want a clarification on it. I would read the question and answer, just to -- not to quote out of context. The Prosecutor said -- asked you: "Were you able to ascertain when prisoners first began to arrive from Bratunac on the Grbovci school?" Sorry for the pronunciation. I don't know the language. And you answered: "According to the survivors, et cetera, et cetera, arrived early in the morning." In the morning of which day, please?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, this information is based on the testimony of one survivor, who was separated at Potocari, taken to the White House. From there, he was transported by bus or truck - I don't remember - to this so-called Hangar in Bratunac, where he stayed for the end of the day. He spent the night there. I got from the details that he will forward about the night that he did spend there, and around midnight, so at the end of the day of 13 July, so early 14 July, he was then transported to the Grbovci school, where he arrived probably - I don't know exactly, but I would make an assessment around maybe 10.00 in the morning, or earlier maybe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. So this arrived early in the morning of July 14; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. July 14th is the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We want to thank Mr. Ruez on behalf of Mr. Blagojevic and the rest of Mr. Blagojevic's Defence team for his testimony here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. We'd like to also show Mr. Ruez our appreciation for being here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. de la Torre? MS. DE LA TORRE: Nothing further from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender from the Prosecution side? MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour. We have provided a list to the court, as well as to Defence counsel, of all of the exhibits that we are offering to the testimony of Mr. Ruez, and they are Prosecution Exhibits 1 through 26 inclusive of all the subpoints. In that regard, Your Honour, we would point out in request, for example, with regard to Mr. Jokic's interview, Ms. Sinatra read portions of that interview to the court, and we would simply request that prior to ruling on its admissibility, that the court read the transcript in its entirety. Because, for example, Ms. Sinatra pointed out where Mr. Jokic called the Prosecutor judges; however, she failed to follow up with the paragraph where Mr. McCloskey explains the distinction between prosecutors and judges to Mr. Jokic. Rather than have the witness simply read that portion of the transcript, we would just request that the court read it for itself in its entirety. Your Honour, at this time we would offer all of those exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do have several objections. Of course, before I questioned Mr. Ruez, I asked that the court not think that we're waiving our right to object to the admissibility of the statement, and we would prefer that the Trial Chamber wait until we've determined the legality of the procedures used during the taking of the statement of Mr. Jokic. And there are two here that they're trying to introduce. We object to the admissibility of, I guess, P26.1/A, 26.1/B, 26.2/A and 26.2/B. And further, I did read the answer into the record of how -- no -- I take it back. I did not. But we will clarify that. When I take further witnesses, I will make sure that we will try to elucidate on these issues about the legality of the statement. Further, I do object, and they're not marked in the Prosecution Exhibit list, the freelance videographer that was Serbian. His name was Goran Petrovic. Mr. Ruez had testified earlier, in an earlier trial, that he didn't give them these videotapes. They were seized and they were not in total and they're not verified, and the Prosecution doesn't mark which ones were taken by Zoran Petrovic, but I think there's a big difference between the OTP investigators' video footage and that of Mr. Petrovic, who was not voluntarily given and his credibility was questioned by Mr. Ruez himself. And it's not clear from their markings on the videotapes or summaries which ones include clippings from Mr. Petrovic. Additionally, we would like to object to the comments and the editorialisation by the Prosecution. If they want to introduce some photographs that are like P-8.8 through P-8.12, the photographs, I think, are aerial photos, but they're of some kind of truck there. We listened to the testimony. It does not say that it was the arrival of bulldozers. That was not clear from Mr. Ruez's testimony, and I think the Prosecution is testifying by leaving these editorials in their exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is an important question. Why didn't you reach it during your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't expect them to be putting his supposition that it could have been the arrival of bulldozers in this exhibit list. I didn't expect them to be annotating it with their comments on -- if it says trucks near Kravica warehouse, that's one thing, but seeing a truck doesn't mean that it was the arrival of bulldozers. And I guess I missed it. Well, I'm going to be honest with you. I didn't cross-examine him on that because I didn't think that the Prosecution would be putting the annotations down here. It's clearly an aerial picture of some trucks on July 5th, but it was not clear that it was the arrival of bulldozers. And those are my only objections at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. de la Torre, would you please tell me which part of the videotapes were taken from that freelancer, Petrovic. I'm sorry. MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour. The videotape -- the compilation videotape actually prior to each particular clip does cite the source, as well as the transcript, which we have provided both to the court and to the Defence, clearly indicates prior to each segment where the footage came from, for example, whether or not it came from Reuters versus Antelope Films versus Petrovic video, which you might recall having seen on the tape itself. So we believe we have clearly indicated where this footage comes from and which is attributable to Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that we did object to the introduction of Mr. Petrovic's video clips earlier, and because it marks it in their summaries or their video clips doesn't mean that it's still admissible. We recognised it when they played. I reserved a running objection on Mr. Petrovic's clippings. And I'm not saying that the whole videotape that they're trying to introduce should not be admissible, but the portions of Zoran Petrovic's clippings should not be admissible, and we object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this Trial Chamber also has some concerns about that three interviews introduced by the Prosecutor into the evidence. Procedurally speaking, at the Pre-Trial Conference, I specifically asked the exhibit list be filed one or two days before the witness begins testimony. In this case, I believe that three interviews and its attached documents do not appear on the first proposed exhibit list for this witness. It was added later. Substantially speaking, one witness could not have the right to cross-examine the other witness on the substance of the interviews without interfering with his right to remain silent. Of course, during the procedures, we ask many questions about this witness, the present witness, about the context in which the interview was conducted, and we are satisfied with the direct examination and the cross-examination. But the problem is about the contents, the contents of those interviews. We found they're very incriminalised materials in it. If without the opportunity for the Defence counsel to directly cross-examine the particular person who gave the interviews, I think it is prejudiced against the interests of their client. So under the Rule 89(D), "the evidence may be excluded if the probative value is substantively outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." So we decided to have those three interviews, as well as attached maps and documents, frozen at this moment, in a refrigerator, not in a coffin, of course. If in the future the Defence team has the opportunity to cross-examine the accused or the accused himself give up his right to remain silent, the Prosecutor could reintroduce those documents through that witness, taking into consideration of the testimony given by this witness today about the context in which those interviews were conducted. So we decided that the documents from P25 to the end are not admitted at this stage. As for the videotapes, we saw it from the proceedings, and we found those videotapes are relevant to this case and has the probative value. So they are admitted into the evidence. Could I make my position clear, that is, the document tendered by the Prosecution, from 1.1 until P24 admitted. It is so decided. Are there any documents from the Defence team that they would like to tender at this stage? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did introduce three -- two documents today through this witness. One is the RS letter from the Defence Ministry that was addressed to -- I don't have it in front of me, Your Honour. I'm sorry. But the RS letter talking about the illegality of the interrogation process by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you remember the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: D2/3. I'm sorry. We would like to move that it be admitted into evidence to show the situation and the problems under Rule 95 with the interrogation and interviews of Mr. Jokic, and it was verified by the witness that he -- he's the one that first mentioned it and brought it up or we wouldn't have known about it. So he was fully aware and can verify the authenticity of the letter. And then D3/3 is the French parliamentary commission interview with Mr. Ruez, and we would like to introduce that document into evidence also. The reason is because it shows conclusions, bias, and suppositions on the part of the witness. It attacks his credibility, we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution? MS. DE LA TORRE: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning the document D2/3, that is the letter, we believe that this document is related to that three interviews. So since those three interviews are not admitted at this stage, we'll consider this document, D2/3, together with that three interviews at a later stage. So this document is not admitted at this stage. But Defence team has the full right to reintroduce it at a later stage. Concerning the document D3/3, since there's no objections from the Prosecution, it is admitted into the evidence. Mr. Karnavas, do you have any documents to introduce?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. All of us wish you a very good luck in your future work. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, My Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. De la Torre. MS. DE LA TORRE: Your Honour, we just -- I'd just like one clarification with regard to the statements that we had offered, and then we do have a few other points we would like to make prior to recessing for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. MS. DE LA TORRE: And I believe I understand the court's ruling with regard to those statements. However, I just wanted to clarify that the Prosecution's intention in offering the statement of Mr. Obrenovic is to allow the Defence access to that information prior to his testimony. He will be a witness in this case, and we do expect that that information be made available to the Defence for the purposes of cross-examination. With regard to Mr. Jokic, the Prosecution is solely offering that particular statement or those - I'm sorry - two statements against Mr. Jokic, and does not intend to offer that for the purposes of any evidence against Mr. Blagojevic in this case. So I just wanted to make the Prosecution's position clear on the intent behind our offering of that particular evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to comment on the fact that the statements of Mr. Obrenovic have already been provided to the Defence, so we don't need to admit those into evidence, and the best evidence will be that Mr. Obrenovic will be coming to testify himself. So I agree with the Court's position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any else? MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. MS. DE LA TORRE: Just a few matters, the first of which, just to clear up the record with regard to the Jokic Defence's claim that they had not been provided the Rule 61 hearing. We did research our records and found that that was provided to them on July 18th, 2002. We did, however, pursuant to the Court's instruction, provide them with a duplicate courtesy copy. We also, Your Honour, have requested in this case reciprocal discovery. To date we have received none. We would request that prior to a witness's testimony, if the Defence intends to use documents or other pieces of evidence in the course of its cross-examination, that they provide that to the Prosecution in advance. If it's something that the Prosecution has provided to them, we would simply ask that they identify it for the Prosecution prior to the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in advance, what do you mean by in advance? Because we have made a ruling that they should furnish us with the documents they have the intention to use during the cross-examination before they cross-examine that witness, and the use that they want. Are we in the same line of thinking? MS. DE LA TORRE: Yes, Your Honour, that we would request that when they provide the material to the court, that they also provide a copy to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. MS. DE LA TORRE: And, Your Honour, prior to the break, we would also like to raise the unresolved issue of Mr. Blagojevic's representation. The undisputed evidence before this Trial Chamber is that Mr. Blagojevic and his counsel are not communicating with one another, nor is Mr. Blagojevic receiving any documents or other pieces of evidence from his counsel. We believe that this puts the Prosecution in an awkward position. We have a continuing discovery obligation, we have documents that we continue to need to tender to the defendant, and at this point, if Mr. Blagojevic and his counsel are not communicating and he's not receiving material, we don't know who to provide that material to. Do we provide it to Mr. Blagojevic directly, to Mr. Karnavas, knowing that Mr. Blagojevic is then not receiving it, or provide copies to both? We believe, Your Honour, that while in one sense this is a matter between Mr. Blagojevic and his counsel, it does affect the integrity of the trial, and we believe, as a result, that we would encourage the court on this break to attempt to resolve that issue, that it's a continuing ethical and legal problem that persists, and we believe affects the continuation of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as you know that before the start of this proceedings, I specifically advised Mr. Blagojevic for him to accept independent counsel on this particular matter. And I have been informed that the Registrar is kind enough to appoint independent counsel, and in the coming week, that counsel will get in touch with Blagojevic. And I also promised to Mr. Blagojevic, once he had some contacts with that independent counsel, we might hold an ex parte hearing on this issue to hear from Mr. Blagojevic what is his specific reasons for this request. We will try our best to solve this issue during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just be heard, because I think the Prosecutor, which is the same Prosecutor that tried to get me to fire Ms. Tomanovic from the Defence case has intentionally misled the court today. She knows very well, very well, that documents are being provided to Mr. Blagojevic. Every single document that we receive in B/C/S, we copy and we provide it to him. If Mr. Blagojevic has chosen not to look at these documents, that's a different matter, but I personally have given him a computer so he can research. I personally bought him a tape-recorder so he can listen to tapes. We've given him every single document, and I had a conversation with the Prosecutor, the Chief Prosecutor, and he knows that the material is being turned over, and I cannot understand why Madam Prosecutor would stand up and falsely go on the record to say that we are not providing the disclosure material to Mr. Blagojevic. And I just want the record very, very clear on this matter. And I do agree with the Trial Chamber, in their aspect of appointing an independent counsel. And as I've indicated, we're prepared to withdraw from the case at the court's pleasure. Until then, we're obligated to do our duty, and I believe that we're doing it as best we can. I also -- I should also add that prior to the situation with Mr. Blagojevic, the record will -- the records will show that, I would say, in the average of two to 300 hours spent with Mr. Blagojevic in consultation in going over all of the documents, and that's between myself and Ms. Tomanovic, with Mr. Blagojevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your statement. I think it's registered in the transcript. Another matter is the oral motion for the access to OTP mission requests. Yes. Yes, Ms. de la Torre. Do you have anything to add? I hope that debate will not last long. MS. DE LA TORRE: No, Your Honour. I just simply I believe the court is in possession of a copy, as is the Prosecution, of a memorandum from the commander of the Detention Unit informing all of the parties that Mr. Blagojevic is refusing to accept legal documentation and other items from his lead counsel, Mr. Karnavas. This is the information that we are relying on, as well as Mr. Karnavas's representation to the Prosecution that he and his client are not communicating with one another, and obviously that's our concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll continue. As for the oral motion for access to the OTP's mission request, during the proceedings, both Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Sinatra made a request to get that mission requests from the Prosecution. We studied this matter during the break, and we found that the mission requests clearly appear to fall within the scope of the Rule 70(A), which are not subject to disclosure obligation under Rule 66 and 67. So their requests are denied. As for the break, I mean the court recess, we believe that a lot of the latest development may affect the proceedings of this Tribunal. We have the -- we'll have a newly amended indictment in this case, and the Prosecution indicated Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic will testify in this proceedings. And Mr. Blagojevic need to solve the issue of the counsel. Taking all those factors into consideration, we decided to have court recess for a month. We'll resume on the 23rd of June, Monday. I hope during this break we could deal a lot of things. This Trial Chamber will request the Prosecution to submit the statements of Mr. Obrenovic and Nikolic 25 days before their testimony. As for the amended indictment, the Prosecution indicated that they would file that application by tomorrow. We'll give ten days from tomorrow to the Defence team for their response, and after that, the Trial Chamber will make a decision concerning the indictment, so as to remove the so-called fundamental flaw of law. Are there anything else the parties would like to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber at this stage? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We won't be seeing Ms. de la Torre after today, Your Honour. I just wanted you to know that. She will be going on maternity leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you coming back? MS. DE LA TORRE: No, Your Honour. There's nothing further from the Prosecution. And no, I will not be returning after today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is we wish you good luck. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's all I was going to say. I can't wait to see the pretty little baby girl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, having said that, we are adjourned until 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
